notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Matthew 22:1–23. I ran out of searches before reaching any Catholic or Orthodox site, bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org, or any page on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching, so those views are missing. The only early-church reading below is Augustine's, and only as the Pulpit Commentary reports it. I read Ellicott in full only up to v. 17, and found nothing useful on vv. 18–19 beyond Guzik.

**v. 1**
- Jesus' answer was aimed at what his opponents were thinking, since they had already been silenced, and he can read thoughts (Matthew Henry). Jesus answered, not to what his opposers said (for they were put to silence), but to what they thought — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_022.cfm
- Guzik: Jesus kept warning the religious leaders and the crowds of the danger of rejecting Him. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-22/

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: The king is none other than God, and the wedding is that between Christ and His Church. The guests who answer the call are themselves, taken together, the bride. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/22.htm
- Barnes: the Greek word means the wedding feast, not just the ceremony. The king here doubtless represents God providing for the salvation of the world. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/matthew-22.html
- Pulpit Commentary: Christ is the Bridegroom. The Church is the bride. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/matthew-22.html

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: as in the vineyard parable, the servants stand for the prophets up to John the Baptist, and the first invitation went to the Jews. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/22.htm
- Wesley's Notes: those invited are Namely, the Jews. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/22.htm
- Guzik: turning down a royal wedding makes no sense, which shows there is no *logical* reason people refuse God's gifts. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-22/
- *Contending for the Faith*: the servants may be John, Jesus and the Twelve, though Lenski disagrees. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ctf/matthew-22.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik, citing Barclay: guests were invited ahead of time, then summoned when everything was ready. "All things are ready" is the gospel: You don't come to God's feast and prepare your own meal. He has made it ready for you; you come to receive. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-22/
- Ellicott: the slaughtered animals echo Isaiah 25:6 and picture the peace and joy Christ offers. The word "dinner" means a morning or midday meal. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/22.htm

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: this is the neglect that brushes off God's kingdom in favour of worldly interests. A second response, open hostility, ran alongside it. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/22.htm
- The *Biblical Illustrator* names four responses to the gospel: ignored, violently rejected, accepted only for show (the man without the garment), and sincerely accepted. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/22-8.html

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: the Greek means deliberate outrage. The parable looks back to the prophets and forward to Christian preachers and martyrs. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/22.htm

**v. 7**
- Guzik reads this as a prophecy of what would happen to Jerusalem. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-22/
- Ellicott: it was first roughly fulfilled when Jerusalem was destroyed, and again whenever nations or churches are punished for unbelief. "Troops" is a better translation than "armies." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/22.htm

**v. 8**
- Spurgeon: they judged themselves unworthy of eternal life, others must be called. Salvation is not a matter of worthiness, or none would be saved. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-22-commentary-spurgeon
- Clarke: they were unworthy because they made light of the invitation and preferred earthly things. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/matthew-22.html

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: "crossroads" literally means where roads meet. He sees a prophecy of the call to the Gentiles, as in Acts 13:46. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/22.htm
- Bible Hub summary: the people from the streets stand for Gentiles and outcast Jews. — https://biblehub.com/matthew/22.htm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: "both evil and good" shows that (1) the gospel is offered to everyone, whatever their past sins, and (2) the visible church holds good and evil mixed together, as in the parable of the net. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/22.htm
- Guzik: this is a parable about grace. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-22/

**v. 11 – the wedding garment** (this is where traditions differ most)
- *Was a garment handed out?* Barnes says hosts supplied robes. Ellicott thinks the story assumes that custom, but adds that either way the man could easily have had one, so the fault was his. Guzik says scholars disagree and there is no evidence of the practice in Jesus' day. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/matthew-22.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/22.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-22/
- *Gill (Calvinist Baptist):* the garment is not good works or any grace of the Spirit, but the righteousness of Christ credited to the believer. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/22-11.html
- *Wesley (Methodist):* The righteousness of Christ, first imputed, then implanted. He adds that the verse is about the last day, not the Lord's Supper. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/22.htm
- *Clarke (Methodist):* people miss out because they do not ask the host for the garment, which is that holiness without which none can see the Lord. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/matthew-22.html
- *Ellicott (Anglican):* he notes that some take the garment to mean baptism and others Christ's imputed righteousness. He calls both "too narrow and too technical." His view: it is holiness (Hebrews 12:14), which Christ gives to whoever truly believes. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/22.htm
- *Spurgeon (Baptist):* the man stands for people who claim to be Christians but do not honour Christ, his sacrifice or his Word. Spurgeon elsewhere says the dress is freely provided for you. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-22-commentary-spurgeon ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/matthew-22.html
- *Desiring God (Reformed Baptist):* The wedding feast is an open invitation, but there is a dress code. Everyone is welcome at the table, but the table changes us. — https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/dont-be-a-wedding-crasher
- *Pulpit Commentary's survey of views:* some say the garment must be something outward, such as baptism, the sacraments or public confession. Others see faith, or faith with love: Augustine wrote "Habete fidem cum dilectione… ista est vestis nuptialis" ("have faith with love; that is the wedding garment"). Others see good works, humility, or purity worked by the Spirit. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/22-11.htm
- *Contending for the Faith:* reading it alongside Revelation 19:8, the garment is "the righteous acts of the saints." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ctf/matthew-22.html

**v. 12**
- Pulpit: "Friend" signals only acquaintance, not affection; Jesus uses the same word to Judas. — https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/matthew-22.html
- Ellicott: "speechless" is the same verb as "put to silence" in v. 34, literally the silence of someone gagged. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/22.htm
- Vincent: the Greek "not" here is a different word from the one in v. 11. It points to the man's attitude, not just how he looked. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/22-12.htm

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: the bright, joyful bridal hall is set against the midnight darkness outside. The words "take him away" (in the KJV) are missing from many of the best manuscripts. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/22.htm
- Clarke: Jewish weddings were held at night in a brightly lit hall, so the "outer darkness" is the darkness just outside. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/matthew-22.html
- Guzik: the indifferent, the hostile and the unchanged all end up the same way. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-22/

**v. 14 – called vs. chosen** (Reformed and Wesleyan readings differ)
- *Spurgeon (Calvinist):* the call goes to everyone who hears, but it does not reach every heart with power. The few find the feast by the choice of God's grace. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-22-commentary-spurgeon
- *Wesley:* Many hear; few believe. Yea, many are members of the visible, but few of the invisible Church. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/matthew/22.htm
- *Ellicott:* within the parable, being "chosen" depends on how people answer the call. Election by God's foreknowledge (1 Peter 1:2) is "not here within view," though it follows from that foreknowledge. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/22.htm
- *T. Arnold (Anglican, in the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary):* this is not an arbitrary call and choice. God sadly rejects many because we would not render ourselves fit for it. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/22-8.html
- *Guzik (Calvary Chapel):* the verse holds human choice and God's choosing together. They stayed away because they refused, and because they were called but not chosen. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-22/
- *Barnes:* the saying sums up the whole parable, not just the episode of the garment. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/matthew-22.html

**v. 15**
- Ellicott: "trap" literally means ensnare. They plotted in secret because Jesus was still popular. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/22.htm
- Guzik: Pharisees teaming up with Herodians shows how much they hated Jesus. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-22/

**v. 16**
- Ellicott: we know the Herodians only from Matthew and Mark. They were supporters of Herod's family, most likely in favour of submitting to Rome. Their flattery unintentionally admits that Jesus was truthful and fearless. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/22.htm
- Guzik, quoting Trapp: Here is a fair glove, drawn upon a foul hand. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-22/

**v. 17**
- Ellicott: the question was built as a dilemma. Saying yes would make him look like a traitor to the people; saying no would put him at odds with Rome. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/22.htm
- Guzik, citing France and Carson: "lawful" means under God's law. This was the poll tax, which Zealots called a badge of slavery. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-22/

**vv. 18–19**
- Guzik: Jesus stays in control and exposes their hypocrisy. Citing Barclay, the poll tax cost a denarius a year. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-22/

**v. 20**
- GotQuestions: Jews regarded such images as idolatry under the second commandment, which was one more danger in answering "yes." — https://www.gotquestions.org/render-to-Caesar.html
- Barnes: the coin normally carried the reigning ruler's likeness and titles. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/matthew/22-20.html

**v. 21**
- Guzik: government makes legitimate demands, and we owe obedience in civil matters (1 Peter 2:17). "Render" means "give back," like paying a debt (France). Because we bear God's image, we belong to God. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-22/
- Clarke: the saying distinguishes the jurisdiction of the two empires of heaven and earth. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/matthew/22-21.html
- GotQuestions: Jesus was drawing a sharp distinction between two kingdoms. — https://www.gotquestions.org/render-to-Caesar.html
- *Lutheran (LCMS devotional):* Christ himself is the coin stamped with God's image. He pays the price by dying under Caesar's law. Jesus is both the spender and the coin, even as He is both priest and sacrifice. — https://in.lcms.org/the-image/
- Gill: the coin was probably from Tiberius's reign. — https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/esv/matthew/22-21.html

**v. 22**
- GotQuestions: hearing this, his enemies marvelled and left. — https://www.gotquestions.org/render-to-Caesar.html

**v. 23**
- Ellicott (as given on Bible Hub): the Sadducees were largely upper-class priests. They denied resurrection because they found it nowhere in the Law. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/22-23.htm
- Gill and Barnes: they also denied angels, spirits and the soul living on after death. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/22-23.htm
- Calvin: Luke shows they denied both bodily resurrection and the immortality of the soul. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/22-23.html
- Ligonier: It was once thought that the Sadducees read only the five books of Moses as Scripture, but we are increasingly sure that they received the entire Old Testament canon. They accepted only doctrines provable from the Pentateuch. This differs from Guzik, who says they accepted only Moses. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/marriage-resurrection ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-22/
- Pulpit: still Tuesday of Holy Week. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/22-23.htm
